newsitem.title: PERU: Peru rebels fear attack, suspend hostage talks.
newsitem.headline: Peru rebels fear attack, suspend hostage talks.

text.p: Marxist rebels holding 72 hostages abruptly suspended talks to end the 79-day crisis, claiming on Thursday they feared the government planned to storm the Japanese ambassador's home.

Rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini said he had evidence the government aimed to rescue the hostages while he and his second-in-command, Rolly Rojas, attended negotiations at a safehouse across the street from the diplomatic residence.

"Tomorrow (Friday) we are not going to attend the negotiations because the right conditions do not exist for a transparent process," the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) leader said in a walkie-talkie interview from within the residence.

"All of a sudden they are waiting for us to leave to start an attack, taking advantage of our absence," Cerpa said. "Without doubt (there is) a tactic to attack from the outside to complement an internal infiltration."
"We have been hearing noises from underneath the residence's floor," Cerpa added, hinting he believed Peruvian security forces were building tunnels to enter the residence in the case of an attack.
Security force sources confirmed the existence of at least four tunnels that were dug while music blasted from loudspeakers outside the besieged residence.
The tunnels would be used in the case of an eventual attack, which would last about seven minutes and would result in many deaths, they added.
Cerpa said the rebels would not return to the negotiating table until the security situation "was cleared up" with the commission of guarantors overseeing talks.
Soon after Cerpa's statements, two guarantors -- Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani and Canadian ambassador Anthony Vincent -- entered the residence.

The office of Peru's negotiator, Domingo Palermo, said the government had no comment on Cerpa's announcement, which marked the first time a round of talks has been called off since negotiations started Feb. 11.

The rebels and government had been expected to spend Thursday mulling the proposals each side presented at the last face-to-face talks on Wednesday. Friday's talks would have been the 10th round of negotiations.
After the MRTA's unenthusiastic reaction to Cuba's offer of asylum, attention in the negotiations had focused on Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori's "all-inclusive" proposal for the rebels.
Palermo and Cerpa formally exchanged their respective proposals on Wednesday, but the guarantors did not reveal the contents of those proposals.
"Both sides have concluded the presentation of proposals and have responded to various questions put forward by the commission of guarantors in order to clarify some points," Vincent said.
Wednesday's meeting held the prospect of the start of real bargaining after Fujimori's announcement that an all-encompassing proposal would be put to the MRTA.
The president was looking to inject some life into the negotiations after the rebels poured cold water on plans to lure them out with an offer of asylum from Cuban leader Fidel Castro.

The rebels stormed the residence Dec. 17 and seized hundreds of cocktail party guests. They released most in the weeks after the attack but still hold their most prized bargaining chips, including Fujimori's brother, Pedro, two government ministers, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia, and two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
